# Two indices of policy space

<p class="lede">The Policy Buffers Index and the Effective Space Index, from
<em>Room to Respond</em>. Pick countries from the map or the search box, choose an
index, and set the year range to compare them over time.</p>

<div class="ps-notes rule-top">
  <p class="mono eyebrow">How the indices are built, and what they cannot see</p>

  <p><strong>Policy Buffers Index (PBI).</strong> An equal-weighted average of six observable
  components: the inverse debt ratio, the fiscal balance, the real policy rate, the current
  account balance, foreign reserves over GDP, and the inverse long-rate spread over the United
  States as a market-access measure. Each is signed so higher means more room, converted to a
  within-year percentile rank before averaging. No estimation is involved, so anyone can audit
  it.</p>

  <p><strong>Effective Space Index (ESI).</strong> The within-year percentile rank of an
  effective-space score from an honest causal forest trained on banking-crisis severity, using
  the Laeven and Valencia (2026) chronology over 1970 to 2019. It changes both the recipe and
  the ingredients relative to the PBI.</p>

  <p><strong>Coverage.</strong> Just under 200 economies, from the late nineteenth century to
  2024, with far thinner coverage in the earlier decades than in recent ones.</p>

  <p><strong>What is plotted here is not the raw estimate.</strong> The series on this page
  have been adjusted and smoothed, and are coarser than the estimates in the paper. They should
  be read for shape and broad position rather than for precise values, and anyone needing the
  underlying figures should work from the paper.</p>

  <p class="ps-caveat-h">How to read these numbers</p>

  <p>Both indices are within-year percentile ranks, so a score is a country's position among
  those reporting in that year rather than a quantity of fiscal space, and a country can move
  simply because others did. Coverage is uneven and thinner in earlier years and outside the
  advanced economies, inputs arrive with error and reporting lags, and countries can be scored
  on partial information, so neighbouring ranks are not meaningful distinctions. The indices
  can only reward what their inputs measure, which leaves out capacities such as reserve
  currency status, standing swap lines, deep domestic investor bases and institutional
  strength — an omission that mechanically favours some countries over others and produces
  individual rankings the paper itself treats as implausible. The estimated index carries
  materially more uncertainty than the observable one, is sensitive to specification, and is
  presented as a companion to it rather than a replacement. The series shown here have been
  adjusted and smoothed, so they are coarser than the underlying estimates, and rankings will
  not line up with the tables in the paper, which restrict the sample. All of
  it is preliminary and may be revised at any time, without notice and without the charts on
  this page being marked as changed. Read the paper before drawing conclusions from any single
  country's series.</p>

  <p class="ps-src">Source: author's calculations, from <em>Room to Respond</em>.

  judgement on the legal status of any territory. Northern Cyprus, Somaliland and Kosovo are
  absent from the basemap as they carry no ISO 3166-1 alpha-3 code.</p>
